subtopic: NATO SECURITY SCREENING
NATO SECURITY SCREENING
speechtext:
1.	Which NATO allies insist on a house to house check of neighbours before individuals have access to NATO information?
2.	Does Canada make similar demands of our NATO allies before non-Canadian NATO personnel are given access to Canadian information and, if so, which NATO allies?
3.	When adverse information is received about an individual from any source, is an opportunity given to that individual to refute or explain the circumstances before a decision is reached?

subtopic: NATO SECURITY SCREENING
speechtext:
1 and 2. All parties to the north Atlantic treaty subscribe to a security agreement which requires them to protect each other's classified information. A common minimum standard of security procedures, methods and techniques has been established and adopted by all parties to the treaty. Each party is responsible for the security clearance of its own nationals irrespective of where they may be employed. Details of these arrangements which Canada has with its allies are matters of confidential agreement which it would not be in the public interest to disclose.
3.	In some cases, when adverse information about an employee is received from sources which are secret and sensitively placed, it is impossible to discuss the information with him in order that he be given an opportunity 28902-5-377
to refute or explain it, either before or after a decision is reached. The reason, of course, is that divulging the information would jeopardize the source and his continuing ability to provide information essential both to the process of determining the degree of confidence which can be placed in employees being appointed to sensitive positions, and to obtaining continuing and accurate information about subversive organizations in Canada. In the majority of cases, however, where the source or sources of the adverse information are either public or capable of being adequately protected, the employee will be interviewed and given an opportunity to explain or refute the adverse information.

speechtext:

Answer: 1, 2 and 3. As the Minister of Justice announced in Banff, on September 6, 1963 and at Quebec city on October 19, 1963, it is the intention of the government to convene a federal-provincial conference next year to seek agreement on an amendment to the British North America Act under which all amendments to the constitution may be made in Canada, and such further amendments as are necessary to meet the needs of today and to reflect the new concept of cooperative federalism. Agreement with the provinces to an amendment to the British North America Act is required to accomplish these objectives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: RESTRICTIONS ON STOCK HOLDINGS OF LIFE INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
The following information relates to Canadian life insurance companies supervised by the federal department of insurance.
(a) The total book value of investments of a company in common shares shall not exceed 15 per cent of the book value of the total assets of the company; (b) not more than 30 per cent of the common shares and not more than 30 per cent of the total issue of the shares of any corporation shall be purchased by any company; (c) a company shall not invest in its own shares and shall not invest its life insurance funds in the shares of any company transacting the business of life insurance; (d) except as described in paragraph (e) shares eligible for investment must have had a record of a dividend payment amounting to at least 4 per cent of the average value at which the shares are carried in the capital stock account of the issuing corporation in each year for a period of seven years preceding the date of investment; (e) a company may invest in common shares not meeting the dividend requirements described in the preceding paragraph and in other investments not specifically authorized but the total so invested may not exceed 5 per cent of the book value of the total assets of the company.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS ZONING POLICY
speechtext:
1. In accordance with the principles of the National Parks Act and national parks purpose, most of the land area in each park is to be retained in a wilderness and near wilderness state. The act provides that these unique natural areas shall be preserved, yet at the same time they are to be made available for the use, benefit and enjoyment of the public. Reconciling these two objectives and solving the problem of a proper balance between character and intensity of public activity and the ability of various regions in a park to support such use without impairment of the natural resource is the crux of the planning objective.
The solution to this problem and the basis of long range planning is the zoning concept. The purpose of zoning is to give order to planning and development by delineating the most appropriate use for each area and setting forth policy objectives for each zone which will ensure protection of the primary

resource yet provide appropriate facilities for public activity, understanding and enjoyment of the attractions.
2.	A preliminary zoning plan has been worked out for the four contiguous mountain parks, Banff, Jasper, Yoho and Kootenay, showing ten wilderness zones encompassing about one third of the area. The remaining two thirds are classed as semi-wilderness. Present and planned facilities associated with access, accommodation and heavy use are contained within the semi-wilderness zones. While the preliminary zoning plan requires further development, current planning is proceeding on the basis of these principles.
3.	Yes, as far as it may be reasonably applicable to each park, considered individually. In the smaller parks, large wilderness zones will not be possible, but even these parks afford scope for setting apart natural areas managed and used for public enjoyment in much the same manner as the wilderness zones in the larger national parks.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. This morning's press carries a report from the United Nations saying that under heavy pressure Canada has given up on an attempt to preserve a formal commonwealth role in the United Nations. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: COMMONWEALTH SEAT ON SECURITY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to give my hon. friend a reply to that question. The debate in the United Nations assembly on the question of enlargement and equitable representation in United Nations councils is to end tomorrow, and when the Secretary of State for External Affairs returns he may wish to report more fully on the results of that debate.
Meanwhile I can say that the question of future representation on United Nations councils is not likely to be solved at this session of the assembly because the Soviet delegation indicated that it would not ratify the amendments to the charter which would permit enlargement of those councils, especially the security council, and that kind of enlargement would go a long way to ensure that the commonwealth would continue to be represented by commonwealth members on the council.
The Soviet delegation links this question to the representation of China, in what I consider to be an unjustifiable stand, and resolutions adopted by the general assembly may not succeed in providing the necessary additional seats for new members from Africa and Asia. In addition, at the present session 55 African-Asian delegations proposed an enlargement of the general committee of the assembly-if you like, the steering committee-from 21 to 24 members, but omitted reference to the commonwealth in that enlargement. As a result of that omission Australia, New Zealand and Canada decided to table an amendment in order to restore this reference to the commonwealth.
I should add, Mr. Speaker, that considerable pressure was brought to bear on the Canadian, Australian and New Zealand delegations to withdraw this amendment, but that pressure was resisted. However, on Saturday
Inquiries of the Ministry last two African members of the commonwealth whose interests were designed to be maintained and protected by this amendment, Ghana and Nigeria, as well as other delegations, appealed during the debate for the withdrawal of this amendment, assuring the movers of the amendment both in the committee and behind the scenes that the commonwealth position would remain unchanged and that the commonwealth would continue to be represented on the general committee.
Under these circumstances Australia, New Zealand and Canada decided not to press the amendment to a vote, which I think was a very wise decision; because if there had been a vote on the resolution to protect the interests of the commonwealth, the commonwealth delegations themselves would have been divided on that vote.

[Editor's Note: Text of the document above referred to is as follows:]
On Saturday morning the Leader of the Opposition inquired about arrangements for financing the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East. He referred to the position of the Canadian delegation as regards a proposal then before the general assembly.
On Friday afternoon the fifth committee of the assembly approved (56-10 Soviet bloc -13) a resolution co-sponsored by Canada, three Scandinavian countries, India and Nigeria, which contained an agreed formula for financing UNEF during 1964. The formula provides that the 1964 costs of UNEF estimated at $17,750,000 will be shared as follows: the first $2 million will be assessed at the regular budget rate; the remainder will also be assessed at this rate, except that the less developed countries will be allowed a 57.5 per cent reduction in their shares. For the past several years, it has been recognized that the less developed countries, having a limited capacity to contribute toward the costs of peace keeping operations involving heavy expenditures, should be allowed reductions in their shares. The gap created by granting these reductions is filled by voluntary contributions from the developed states.
These financing arrangements apply as regards the less-developed countries and are not related to the problem arising from the refusal of the Soviet bloc and some other developed countries to pay their share of the costs. These countries are assessed at the regular scale and their arrears of payment have been accumulating.


At the fourth special session of the assembly last June, the formula for financing both UNEF and ONUC allowed 55 per cent reductions to the less developed countries. The Canadian delegation at the current session was instructed to urge the readoption of the June formula and, in fact, it was adopted for the Congo force. In relation to UNEF, however, the less developed countries pressed for a slightly larger reduction. The voluntary contribution expected of Canada to fill the current gap has not been finally determined but it is estimated to be about $80,000.
Because of the importance which Canada attaches to the role played by UNEF in the Middle East, the government considered it desirable to support the modified formula. In agreeing once more to an ad hoc arrangement, the government has continued to insist that financing arrangements for peace keeping operations must be placed on a long term basis incorporating the principle of collective financial responsibility.

The hon. member referred on that date to some remarks I had made in San Francisco the previous day. He asked what the federal government was doing by way of helping the forest industries to take care of an expected increase in demand. That question covers a wide field, and to answer it would take some

[Editor's note: Text of document referred to above is as follows:]
As the hon. member for Dorchester and the other members of the house are aware, the responsibility for managing the forest industries of the ten provinces and for the sale of forest products generally rests with the industries and the provinces. The responsibility of the federal Department of Forestry is largely in the research field. In so far as my department is concerned, its methods of assisting the forest industries fall into three general categories:
1.	We assist the forest industries directly through forest products research in our two well equipped and well staffed laboratories in Ottawa and Vancouver. The function of the two laboratories is to increase the industries' competitive ability through better wood products and the reduction and profitable utilization of primary waste materials.
2.	The department is currently reviewing its role as a co-ordinator of special forest economics information in an effort to become a more effective and useful partner with industry in this vital area. With its special understanding of the forest industries, the department has embarked on a program of supplying forest economic data to industry that will be of direct and immediate benefit in such matters as increased plant efficiency, marketing research and analyses to provide new uses for wood, the development and exploitation of new markets, and the expansion of existing markets.
3.	We also assist the provinces in securing and maintaining the resource itself through-
(a)	Research on the better production and management of trees and their protection from fire, insects and diseases;
(b)	Co-operative federal-provincial forestry agreements designed to improve access into the forests, fire suppression effectiveness, reforestation activities and various other projects proposed by the provinces which would assist in the preservation of the resource and its optimum utilization by industry. Millions of federal funds have been allocated to these activities over the last decade.
A specific recent example of practical assistance to industry is the $3 million being made available for the expansion of the

research facilities of the pulp and paper research institute of Canada, at Pointe Claire, Quebec.
Another example of our program for greater assistance is the construction at Victoria, B.C., at a cost of nearly $3,000,000 more, of what will be one of the finest forest research laboratories on the continent. This unit is intended to provide constant and up to date practical research information on forest protection and management to that province's great forest industries, as is being done through other departmental laboratories and establishments right across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday last the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) asked a question concerning the grounding of CF-100 aircraft. I am now in a position to answer it.
An investigation which was carried out subsequent to a recent accident involving a CF-100 aircraft revealed that the unsuccessful attempts by both crew members to eject were caused by a technical malfunction of the ejection seats. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Last week I asked the Minister of Transport what progress had been made in an investigation into the quantities of glass which were found in Canadian wheat shipped to the Soviet union. I urged the minister to make a statement as soon as possible in the interests of protecting the good name of Canadian wheat abroad. I wonder if the minister has that report.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. On Saturday last the hon. member asked me a question on this subject with particular reference to the published report of a speech made by the Montreal port manager, Mr. Beaudet. There have been earlier questions on the subject. I think there was one arising out of my statement of December 2, a question by the Leader of the Opposition and another question by the hon. member for Calgary North, as well as one or two others. My answer, therefore, will be a little longer than would otherwise be the case.
An intensive investigation was made into this matter following the receipt of formal notification from the Soviet authorities that glass or bottles had been found in seven vessels going to the U.S.S.R. Two of these vessels had loaded at Montreal, one at Baie Comeau, two at West Saint John, one at Quebec and one took on cargo at both Montreal and Halifax. These vessels loaded during the period from October 12 to November 8.
I have read the reports of Mr. Beaudet's speech and have also spoken to the officials of the department who were present and heard the speech. In its references to this subject it seemed to accurately describe the situation. Reference was made in the speech to the fact that possibly only one hold in each of the seven cargoes had been found to contain glass. This statement was based on a verbal communication in Moscow to the chief inspector of the board of grain commissioners, which suggested that the contaminated grain was merely a part of the cargo and not the entire quantity contained on the seven vessels involved.

The investigation to which I referred earlier was conducted by an interdepartmental group consisting of representatives of the Departments of Agriculture, Transport, Trade and Commerce, and the board of grain commissioners and the national harbours board. Glass was discovered also in four railway carloads recently shipped from water and inland points in Ontario to port elevators.
I have come to the conclusion that it would be extremely difficult if not impossible to determine at this time where and by what means the glass was introduced into the grain. I am of the opinion that the unfortunate incidents were the result of carelessness, perhaps arising in part out of the pressures involved in handling the very large movement. I consider therefore that our efforts now should be mainly concentrated on avoiding a recurrence.
In previous discussion in the house the question has been raised as to where responsibility lies in a matter of this kind. There is no one government agency with complete control or authority and, of course, commercial firms are also involved in the movement of grain. The board of grain commissioners, under the Minister of Agriculture, is responsible for the quality and condition of grain until it is discharged from a licensed elevator into an ocean carrier. The national harbours board, under the Minister of Transport, operates elevators which, like privately owned elevators, are covered by the regulations of the board of grain commissioners. Its responsibility ceases when the grain leaves its elevators. Any change in the quality or condition of grain, or responsibility for the introduction of extraneous material after loading on a vessel, rests with the commercial firms involved in the transactions. It is obvious, therefore, that a number of agencies and private interests are involved in grain handling.
I wish to refer now to steps which are being taken to avoid a recurrence. It must be recognized, first, that some government departments and agencies have staffs working in and around grain handling facilities and have some authority over bottle or glass material on government premises. The board of grain commissioners, the national harbours board and the departments of agriculture and transport have notified their staffs involved in grain handling that the government takes a very serious view of the matter, and that they are not permitted to have glass bottles in any areas where grain is handled. They have been informed what disciplinary action will be taken if employees are found responsible for causing extraneous material to enter grain handling or storage facilities or holds of ships. Additionally, steps are being taken

to prevent the removal of glass containers from canteens on property under government control where grain is handled.
I have also communicated with the commercial interests involved, namely the grain elevator operators, grain carriers, both water and land, shipping agents, stevedoring companies, maritime unions, independent port wardens and harbour commissioners, indicating the government's serious concern and pointing out the possible adverse effects on the economy. These people have been asked to take immediate steps to ensure that glass containers are not used in areas where grain is handled, and to advise the government of the action they are taking to ensure that no extraneous material is allowed to enter grain.
The board of grain commissioners is enacting a regulation, under the authority of the Canada Grain Act, making it an offence for any person wilfully or carelessly to cause or permit glass or other extraneous material to be introduced into or remain in grain, in any elevator or land carrier or in any vessel delivering grain to a destination in Canada.
As the minister to whom the responsibility for co-ordinating this matter has been given, I now appeal to everyone involved, both management and labour, government and private, to do everything possible to avoid careless or thoughtless actions which would damage the reputation of Canadian grain with serious consequent effects on our exports and on the economy as a whole. I am confident that the necessary co-operation will be forthcoming from all concerned. The high reputation and quality of Canadian grain are renowned throughout the world. I trust that with the measures now announced, and with the co-operation of all who are involved in the handling and movement of grain, Canada's record will be even better than in the past. I want to assure the house that this matter will be kept under close surveillance.
I must apologize to hon. members for taking a little longer than I would otherwise in answering this question, but I do believe the subject matter is of such importance to the grain trade and the economy of this country that I had a duty to answer the question fully.

There is one clause that I think deserves consideration, and perhaps the house would allow me to make reference to it now. I refer to clause 10, which provides for the appointments and says:
The commissioner may

I am very glad this is the first step toward the assurance that we shall have in this country a redistribution made without regard to political bias or partisan considerations. We brought this question before the house in 1952. Hon. George Drew moved and I seconded an amendment when the bill was before the house. This amendment was:

It is quite interesting to note the change of opinion that takes place over the years, Mr. Speaker, for I see that those who voted against that amendment in 1952, when we endeavoured to bring about this desirable objective, included the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) among other distinguished members at that time. I was rather surprised today to hear the view expressed by the Minister of Finance, who is rather new to the house, that he was not going to be cross-examined. That was the view of Charles I. I thought it had ended with the unfortunate demise of that king, but apparently that view is still held among those who occupy positions of responsibility on the treasury bench and who are not fully conversant with the traditions of parliament.
I have studied the reports of the commissions appointed in Australia, and they are very revealing. Mr. Castonguay, who it is generally agreed will occupy the position to be created under this bill, visited Australia; and a reading of the reports by the commissioners on the way they have dealt with the matter in their country is of particular interest. I do not see any one of them occupying a position similar to the representation commissioner who belongs to all of the commissions as set up; the reports do not indicate that. But the report of the commissioners of the various states were in general acceptable with one or two exceptions, all of which are set forth in the reports. The grounds of protest are generally those of inequitable distribution of enrolments giving excessive numbers to metropolitan divisions, illogical inclusion of some urban metropolitan districts with adjacent rural areas, and matters such as that. In other words, in Australia the general complaint seemed to be that there was over-representation in the urban areas, a complaint that is the reverse of that sometimes advanced in this country.
Our attitude throughout has been that action should be taken in this regard. The setting up of the commissioner is acceptable. I think that was not the view we held when we were in office, but I am not going to argue that question again. I think a man of the stature and fairness of Mr. Castonguay will make a worth-while contribution toward making parliament more effective.

But, as the Leader of the Opposition is aware, interpretations were placed on statements made earlier by him, or on actions taken earlier by him, which suggested that he was not prepared to go all the way with the proposals for impartial redistribution. He has set aside those doubts. He has referred again to the proposal made in the speech from the throne in the last session in which he was prime minister. He has told us he wants redistribution to be carried out by an impartial body. That is now the position of the present government. It has been our position throughout the years. It is the position taken by other groups. We are all agreed. I hope the day has now come when it will not be necessary for editorial writers to say to any party in the House of Commons: No politics, please, in connection with redistribution. It is up to us. We can demonstrate that we are united in this high purpose, and if we can carry it through it will be a good day for parliament.
I recognize that this is only a first step- that the other piece of legislation will also have to be passed. I recognize we may have difficulties about some of the details in the other bill. We have already indicated some of those difficulties during the earlier debate.
I need not repeat the position we in this party took with regard to some of those details. However, I suggest that differences over detail will not justify anyone saying that anyone is trying to detract from the idea of redistribution by an impartial body. We like, in this House of Commons, to be in a position to attack right and left-to blame the Liberals, to blame the Tories, and that sort of thing. It is a happy thought that today we have no need to do that, and the sooner we make it clear that we are unanimous on this principle of redistribution by an impartial body the better it will be for parliament and for the whole legislative and democratic process in this country. I trust we can get on with this piece of legislation and, having passed it, that we can deal with the other bill at an early date when the new session starts.

Representation Commissioner
It was not clear from what the Leader of the Opposition was saying about the other bill what his attitude is toward its being introduced tomorrow, or some day this week, and being read a first time. I accept his suggestion, despite any previous difficulties we may have had, that the introduction of that bill should be held up until this debate is over. But after this debate is over and after this bill has been passed, I think there might be consent, tomorrow or later this week, to the introduction of the other bill so that it may be printed and we may know what the government has in mind for parliament at the next session.
When we get into committee on this bill there may be a few amendments moved from this part of the house to some of the provisions dealing with the details of the election machinery. We have no amendments to suggest to those features of the bill which deal with redistribution. I did intend to raise a question about clause 22, and I am glad, as I am sure Your Honour will be glad, that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has indicated there will be an amendment to that clause. We are not supposed to refer to clauses of a bill on second reading, but far be it from me to be outdone by the Secretary of State or by the Leader of the Opposition, who have both done so.
Before I am called to order, may I remind hon. members that clause 22 proposes the unusual course that something should be done on a motion in the name of Mr. Speaker. I am sure this is a situation we should try to avoid. We once had something done in this house on the initiative of the Speaker, something which is of sorry memory, six or seven years ago, and I think it would be far better that if a motion has to be made it should be made in the name of the house by the Prime Minister as the leader of the house. So I am glad the Secretary of State does propose to make an amendment with regard to clause 22, the only clause having to do with the redistribution aspect of this bill which we might have sought to amend. With regard to some of the other clauses dealing with the election machinery, we may have suggestions to make.
Because of the unanimity which has been demonstrated on this occasion, we are able to omit references to past history. The fact is we now have the party in power, the party which has been in power, and parties which would like to be in power all agreeing that the time has come for independent redistribution. This is an important step, and we support this bill.
IMr. Knowles.]

Mr. Chairman, as indicated at the second reading stage by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, there are two or three suggestions by way of amendment that I should like to propose to clause 9 which, as was pointed out, really has to do with the instituting of a certain review and study of the methods of registration of electors and methods of absentee voting by electors. The suggestions I wish to make are by way of addition, rather than change in what is now set forth. They have to do generally with the idea that in addition to examining the methods of registration and of absentee voting which may be in effect in other countries the study should also include an examination of the methods followed in respect of these matters in the various provinces of our own country. I do not know what other members of the committee have found the situation to be, but certainly I have had a great many people suggest to me from time to time that we should be moving toward greater uniformity in respect of elections at both the federal and provincial levels. It seems to me that an opportunity is provided under clause 9 at least to consider this idea.
In order not to prolong the discussion I should like to move immediately:
That paragraph (a) of subclause 1 of clause 9 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
5944	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Representation Commissioner
"Review and study methods of registration of electors used in provincial elections and in elections in countries where continuous electoral rolls are maintained."
In line with the suggestion made earlier by the Secretary of State I would hope he will recognize that this amendment is put forward in a completely non-partisan way and I would hope that perhaps he might be the first to indicate his acceptance of the idea put forth in the amendment.

There should be a review and study of the methods of absentee voting used in provincial elections and elections in countries where provision is made for absentee voting. For many years we have had in the province of British Columbia a system of absentee voting in provincial elections. It is one that is considered to be quite satisfactory and which meets the needs of the province. It is one that would be well worth including in this study.
The next suggestion I wanted to put forward has to do with studying the methods of proxy voting used in provincial elections and in elections in other countries. I have been given to understand that one or two of the provinces of Canada do have some arrangements for proxy voting under certain circumstances. I am not familiar with the details, but I have been informed that is the case. The next proposal would need an additional paragraph Cd), if it were put forward in this form. Mr. Chairman, I think what the hon. gentleman has in mind could be brought about by simply leaving out certain words in paragraph (b), to review and study methods of absentee voting by electors, who, by reason of absence, and so on. If you omit those words, it would enable the commissioner to look into a plan, whether provincial or national.
This certainly is a very important matter in so far as those who serve in external affairs, trade offices abroad or where other positions of extraterritorial responsibility are concerned. The people who serve their country abroad, with the exception of those in the armed forces, are placed in a very unenviable position in being denied their full rights

of citizenship. Anything that might be recommended in that connection will be beneficial. Over and over again, as I have visited embassies abroad and met the Canadians who serve their country outside of Canada, I have found that one of the major objections they have to serving abroad is that it denies them the right which is essential to full participation in the government of the country.
I am sure the hon. gentleman will not misunderstand me when I say that I am not impressed by the suggestion that there should be proxy voting in this country. There are enough difficulties in the way now, without adding to them.

Mackenzie King, in the election of 1935, who was visiting a certain province in which one of his grandfathers was buried. During the course of the day he said he would like very much to visit that cemetery. He said, "You know, he was a fine man but he was a Conservative; I never quite understood that. He voted Conservative consistently." The member, who afterwards occupied one of the highest positions on the treasury bench stated, "Don't worry about that, Mr. King; he has been voting in every election." This type of proxy exercise of the franchise is just one of those difficulties in the mind of the Secretary of State, otherwise he would not have impelled me to give that example.

Representation Commissioner would mean quite what he intended to mean. If the paragraph referred to a review and study of methods of registration of electors used in provincial and national elections, in provinces and countries, I think that amendment and the same amendment in paragraph (b), would meet the problem. I am quite sure from what discussion I have been able to have about this matter it was just taken for granted that anything being done in Canada would be studied. This amendment would make sure that it would be done. If there were no objection, I do not see why the hon. member could not move his amendment in amended form to paragraphs (a) and (b). There does not seem to be any disposition not to accept it.
I rather share the view of the Leader of the Opposition in respect of the proxy question, but for an additional reason to the one he has given. It is this: There is a time limit in this measure on these studies. If redistribution is done, and these studies are to be done, the whole business is to be reviewed, according to the provisions of this bill, in 1969. From what I am able to learn these two studies alone are going to take pretty well all the time that is required.
I think it is the unanimous view in the country, at least among those who have anything to do with elections, that if we can find a satisfactory method of having permanent lists to reduce the period of elections, we would all say hurrah. Anyone who values his citizenship, as we all do in this house, must feel that every Canadian citizen should have the opportunity of exercising the most important right of citizenship, the franchise,, if it is possible to arrange to have that done.
These two studies seem to be of such transcendent importance, compared with the question of proxy voting, that I would prefer not to impose this further duty at this time upon the commissioner. If at the time the review takes place there is some feeling we ought to go on having other tasks for a representation commissioner, then it might be considered at that time. This is perhaps somewhat of a conservative approach to the matter, but on this day of unity perhaps I may be permitted to express that.

Mr. Chairman, I think we should do everything possible to assure that everyone has the opportunity to vote and will exercise his right in the future. When I spoke a moment ago about a former prime minister and his grandfather I neglected to say-and I know it was understood by members of the committee-that the member in question with whom Mr. King was travelling said he had been voting Liberal ever

Representation Commissioner since he passed away. Of course none of us want to see that kind of proxy voting practised, but we do wish to encourage people to exercise their vote as far as possible.
I am not one of those who believe in compulsory voting. I do not think it has worked out well. Mr. Castonguay has been in Australia where they have compulsory voting, but in my opinion this idea has not worked out too well.
A few years ago I had a suggestion given to me by an old recluse farmer in Saskatchewan who had a plan whereby everybody would vote. He said that if at the time an elector registered to vote he were required to pay $1 there would be a 100 per cent vote, or as near 100 per cent as possible, provided provisions were made that at the time the elector was handed the ballot he received a counterfoil which would secure him a refund of the $1. While this is a system I do not recommend, it is an example of a citizen who was devoting his thoughts to the solution of a matter that is very difficult, and one that is most costly to all who participate in elections in getting out the voters, while keeping strictly within the law.

MINAS BASIN
speechtext: That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the re-establishment of the Minas basin ferry service with special attention given to the use of a Hovercraft in this operation.

subtopic: MINAS BASIN
speechtext:
Agreed.
5950	HOUSE OF
Minas Basin Ferry Service

subtopic: MINAS BASIN
speechtext:
I would be quite happy to resume my seat if unanimous agreement were given to the adoption of this proposal. However, I feel somewhat doubtful that this is, indeed, the situation and 1 therefore consider it would be wise if I gave the house a little background information to show why I placed this resolution on the order paper.
The Minas basin ferry service was a service available to the people of Nova Scotia in the Annapolis valley, and the town of Parrs-boro in my constituency. This service came to an end in 1940, after 90 years of operation. The federal government of that day considered it necessary to take the ferry which was used to provide this service and employ it in Newfoundland on duties which were considered to be of greater importance. At the time the ferry service was eliminated, there was no great hue and cry either in the Annapolis valley or in my constituency, mainly because it was a tidal operation and the trucking companies considered the type of service which had been provided an outmoded one.
Since that day there has been growing concern among the people of the Annapolis valley and my constituency that a more up-to-date service should be provided. The saving in mileage brought about by a ferry is considerable when one considers the area of Nova Scotia concerned and the time spent by trucking firms and others in going around the Minas basin rather than across it. If this ferry service were re-established it would mean the elimination of about 115 miles of travel, especially for tourists and transportation companies engaged in agriculture and fishing. The introduction of a practical transportation service would, I believe, be of real benefit to my area as well as to other areas associated with the Minas basin and the bay of Fundy.
In two different countries there have been significant advances which have made possible a type of ferry service far more efficient than anything which has gone before. In Britain they have invented the Hovercraft, a new type of craft which is capable of travelling at tremendous speed over water. It can travel as fast as 75 miles per hour, and a great deal of consideration has been given by the government of the United Kingdom to the employment of this type of transportation facility. In Russia there has been a tremendous improvement in public transportation consequent on the development of the hydrofoil, a vessel somewhat similar to the Hovercraft. Both these vessels hover above the surface of the water; they do not actually touch the water and they are capable of tremendous speed. It is my feeling that in a


country such as ours, where so many transportation difficulties are encountered, and so much water has to be traversed, and where there is such a heavy demand for exploration in the northland, the adoption of one or of both these craft might well bring us tremendous advantages, as well as savings from the taxpayers' point of view. They would, of course, need to be capable of moving the heavy transport vehicles which are so much a part of the transportation system of this country today.
In May of this year I had the opportunity to take part in a demonstration of one of these Hovercraft in Montreal and I found myself moved over the St. Lawrence river at 75 miles an hour, an amazing speed when one considers he is moving over water. For that matter, the craft was capable of moving over land, as well, because, in fact, it operates two or three feet above the level of the water, or the land, and obstacles do not present any great problem. I think craft of this type would prove to be of tremendous benefit in operations in northern Canada. I believe, too, that the service I have in mind, the Minas basin ferry service, and the service provided between Digby and Saint John, New Brunswick, could be joined together if craft of the type capable of moving the type of transport we have in our country could be made available. At the same time we would eliminate the heavy cost of wharfage facilities, which faces the government at the present time.
It is my opinion that governments have not been as interested in the development of craft of this type as they should be. When I say that, I am not saying that the former government was any better or more realistic about this matter than the present one. I am simply saying that this government and maybe the provincial governments-because there is certainly a field here where they could become involved-have not in my opinion looked at this subject realistically enough, and have not taken advantage to the extent they should of the tremendous amount of information available today both in Great Britain and Russia, where great amounts of money have been spent to produce some significant vehicles in this field.
In the November, 1963 issue of "Soviet Union Today" there is a description of a hydrofoil motorship which has a seating capacity of 250 to 300 passengers and a cruising speed of 75 kilometers per hour. In England at the present time a Hovercraft is either in the planning stage or being constructed which will be put on the English channel run and will carry approximately 300 passengers.

It is my view that in Nova Scotia, where transportation is so very important, there is an opportunity to eliminate a good deal of the money that is now being paid out in government subsidies and also to eliminate the heavy wharfage problems that are always on the doorstep of the Department of Public Works by endeavouring to have a craft of this type constructed to provide service in the Minas basin, and also between Saint John and Digby. I know that at the present time the new ferry operating between Digby and Saint John is encountering difficulties because of the wharfage facilities at Digby. They simply are not satisfactory for the new ferry that has been placed in the service by the C.P.R. How much better it would be if we could eliminate the wharfage facilities altogether by using a craft that did not need them, and which could provide a much better and more efficient service and eliminate so much time.
There are also other areas in other parts of Canada, certainly along the St. Lawrence river, about which the same thing can be said and probably even to a greater extent. We have heard in recent days in the house about the problems in the Baie Comeau area of Quebec where ferry subsidies are being removed, and because of this the people may be deprived of transportation facilities which they consider they need very badly.

Minas Basin Ferry Service announcements with regard to ferries generally would seem to indicate that the government is going to involve itself in very substantial expenditures of money. It may well be that we are away behind the times and that we could save a great deal of money, having regard to what we are spending in subsidies, maintenance charges and so on and the heavy cost of wharfage facilities, if we would make a thorough investigation into the possibility of using craft of this type, because it might well be that a great deal of benefit would accrue.

subtopic: MINAS BASIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this notice of motion may I say I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), knowing as I do that his area is affected by this problem of a ferry service as is the constituency of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). I was interested in the various points of view and considerations put forward by the hon. member. However, in view of the need of that particular area for transportation I think that the possibilities of the Hovercraft are substantially better than those of the hydrofoil. Each of these types of conveyance has the drawback that it cannot carry a great amount of weight and, as the hon. member has said, one of the real needs between the Annapolis valley and the Parrs-boro-Amherst area is for transportation that can handle trucks and a large amount of freight. The Hovercraft does have the advantage over the hydrofoil that it can operate irrespective of extreme tidal conditions such as prevail in that area.
Transportation across the narrow strips between Cape Blomidon on the Annapolis valley side and the Parrsboro shore on any regular basis has been suspended since before the war, but the transportation that was provided then in the form of a small car ferry would not solve the real need at the present time because I believe the previous ferry could only carry seven or eight cars. This area is considered as one of the potentially great tidal power development areas of the North American continent. The vast amount of water that comes in and goes out

Minas Basin Ferry Service of Minas basin twice daily passes through the narrow gut between Cape Blomidon and Parrsboro with terrific force and it is generally accepted that this could be converted into a tremendous amount of power by a very extensive undertaking of the Passama-quoddy type. However, if that is ever done, that in itself might solve the transportation question across this stretch of water, because a road could be built across any such dam.
In the meantime, I cannot help but recall that Cape Blomidon was supposedly the home of Glooscap, a god of the Micmac tribe which inhabited Nova Scotia. I recall from my school days that he supposedly created two islands by throwing some earth at a beaver that was swimming by. The islands are there now in the bay of Fundy. If Glooscap really existed today, he could probably solve our problem very quickly. Unfortunately, this is not the case, so for a moment we might consider the area that would be served by truck and car transportation across this body of water.
In my view, it would not be of assistance or benefit to the metropolitan Halifax area since the route to Amherst by the main highway through Truro would be a much quicker route than travelling through the Annapolis valley. I think the only transport that would be affected would be the cars going from the Annapolis valley to the Cumberland area. Contrary to what the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) has suggested, this transport would involve no fish products whatever, but agriculture products would be helped if efficient transportation could be provided across this body of water.
In the days that have gone by, investigations have been made into the possibility of a conventional ferry service across this body of water. The problem has always been the cost of wharfage, and this problem arises as a result of the extremely high tides, probably the highest in the world, existing in the area. The cost of wharves would be $6 million or something in that vicinity, whereas the ferry itself would only cost a little over a million dollars. The total cost of this project would thus be in the vicinity of $7 million, and it has never been considered warranted in view of the amount of good this money could do if applied elsewhere to maritime transportation problems. I would comment that if this were the situation today, Mr. Speaker, the higher expenditure of $6 million or $7 million which the hon. member for Cumberland is proposing, would leave us in the same position, where the service

would not be warranted, worthy as it is, in so far as the immediately adjacent areas are concerned.
A Hovercraft service, while it would have a limited possibility in serving truck transport, would nevertheless represent a small investment in wharfage facilities. At any rate, it would probably be the answer to the question of automotive transport and small freight transport in this area. Unless it could take a substantial number of cars, there would be little in way of passenger traffic between points involved, because anyone going from the Annapolis valley, where the towns are spread out, into the Cumberland area, where they are again spread out, would likely be travelling by motorcar. I understand that the latest developments in Hovercraft would enable a reasonable number of cars to be carried across this body of water.
I think, therefore, that the suggestion made by the hon. member has some merit in this respect. It is, of course, not original at this time by any means, because the government of Nova Scotia has been exploring the possibility of a Hovercraft service. In this regard, I might say that since the areas that would be served are entirely within the province of Nova Scotia and the route would be, in essence, an extension of the highway system of that province, it would seem only reasonable to expect the province to participate in the cost of such a service. These few remarks, Mr. Speaker, represent my thoughts on this subject. I do say that the Annapolis valley is today an area of considerable prosperity and with the mixed farming that has developed in that area, the question of getting produce to market or obtaining a new market is of importance. If this ferry service could be established it would enable fresh products from the valley to be moved economically to places in the Amherst and Moncton region, and certainly that would be a step in the right direction. I feel, therefore, that this motion does have merit.

subtopic: MINAS BASIN
speechtext: I feel I should say a few words with regard to this motion by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates). As preceding speakers have said, I feel there is some merit in what he has proposed because transportation in the maritime provinces has, I think, placed us at a disadvantage. I am thinking of purely local areas. However, in so far as the desire for transportation facilities is concerned, there is always the problem of cost involved. In most cases, this is the deciding factor in relation to whether or not the facilities will be provided.

The hon. member for Cumberland gave us the historical background of this Minas basin ferry service. I do not know how many members of the house are familiar with the topography or the geography of the Minas basin area of Nova Scotia. I suggest it would shorten the route if you entered the province of Nova Scotia at the New Brunswick border, at Sackville. If you wanted to go into the Annapolis valley, it would shorten the route by some 100 miles if the service were reinstated from Parrsboro to Wolfville. I believe it is true to say that, not only in the maritime provinces but everywhere, distances have not the same implication today that they had in days gone by.
I am sure that even if the Parrsboro ferry service were in operation today, unless one wanted the experience of going across the Minas basin, it is doubtful if he would take the ferry. The main reason for the trip by ferry would be to see the scenery around the Minas basin, but one could see this scenery if he were to travel by car. I think this is true particularly of the tourists. I do not believe the tourists would take the ferry if they came to the Minas basin, as they generally like to see the countryside through which they are motoring. I do not see a great deal of appeal in it for the tourists, particularly the tourists coming in from Bar Harbour or Saint John because they must cross the bay of Fundy to make the mainland of Nova Scotia, and I know that if they are proceeding to Truro or Cumberland county in Nova Scotia they would not care to embark on another ferry trip, when the distance around the basin is only about 100 miles.
As I listened to the hon. member speaking about the new types of transportation, such as the hydrofoil, the question occurred to me, is this really the type of transportation that is needed? If it is to be of any benefit the type needed is something that will take trucks and motorcars, and I doubt if much benefit would be derived from a purely passenger or light freight service. In that respect I think this whole thing should be given a great deal more consideration.
I would like to see a proposal coming from the government of Nova Scotia because the ferry service is within the provincial boundaries of Nova Scotia. If the province cannot finance it, then I think it should make some proposal to the federal government.
I believe that in prior debates this project was mentioned as something to which the Atlantic development board might give consideration. I do not know whether that board has come up with any suggestion. I do not even know if it has studied the matter; probably it has not because I think it would
Proposed Office of Parliamentary Counsel not have priority among the projects that are presently being considered by it.
I have no desire to block this motion. Actually it only asks the government to give consideration to the project. I do not see anything wrong in giving consideration to it, but I do feel much more study should be undertaken to decide the right type of ferry service that should be provided across the Minas basin, and to determine whether the expenditures would warrant it.
I do not know anything about these hydrofoil, or Hovercraft, but I would imagine that if they are the type that can carry trucks and motorcars they would be very expensive. Another expense involved is the building of wharves and ground development for a day and night service, which would be very expensive, considering that the tides run 30 feet high in the bay of Fundy. I know that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) quoted something like $6 million or $7 million.
I suggest that this matter be thoroughly studied. As I said before, it is the prime responsibility of the government of Nova Scotia, and if representatives of the provincial government, the Atlantic development board and some people from the federal scene got together, then maybe a solution to this Minas basin problem might be found.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED OFFICER TO EXAMINE PUBLIC COMPLAINTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the creation of an office of parliamentary counsel, with objectives and manner similar to the office of ombudsman used in Scandinavian countries such as Sweden and Denmark, for the purpose of examining grievances of Canadian citizens which arise in

Proposed Office of Parliamentary Counsel their relations with the administration of the federal state in Canada, and reporting on the merits of these individual grievances to this house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I see we have 22 minutes to devote to this topic, and I do not know what can really be resolved in that brief time. Just before the sunny Secretary of State departed from the chamber he told me he was in support of this motion personally, but of course he was not speaking for the government.
This subject has been a matter of some discussion for the last several years. I think I first put it on the order paper four sessions ago, but this is the first time there has been an opportunity to debate it. I do not know how important hon. members view it, but I fastened on to the conception because of a number of cases I encountered as a member of parliament and about which I was unable to do anything. I felt the administrators had gone as far as they could, but the individual citizen who had a complaint was still aggrieved and felt his grievance had not been handled impartially. In essence that would be the great advantage of creating this kind of office.
As I say, discussion of the subject has gone on in a lot of journals. Professor Rowat of Carleton University has written a number of articles about it, some in the popular magazine Maclean's, some in the public administration periodical, and in the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science.
Recently New Zealand has adopted the public defender plan. It is on the statute books of that country and is working. The British have examined the matter through a couple of non-partisan committees. The Conservative and the Labour party have groups studying -it, and I have here a report which says the Conservative party in Great Britain indicates general acceptance of the idea. The unofficial group in England that has made a thorough report on it was called JUSTICE. There is a committee formed, largely of people with both political and legal experience who are concerned over the fact that discretionary powers allotted by statute to various boards and agencies have led sometimes to a conflict between individual citizens and the boards or agencies, with an inadequate form of redress or an inadequate form of appeal.
Very recently the royal commission on government organization in its report No. 5 had some statements to make on this very subject. On page 94 the commissioners write:
In addition, because of the growing need for ministerial attention to the difficult problems of policy and the general direction and co-ordination of its execution, the public's recourse to ministers of the review of official acts and redress of
IMr. Fisher.]
minor grievances become less satisfactory. Moreover, because the minister is held politically accountable for all actions of his subordinates and it is the practice in party strife to make issues of such matters-however trivial-the minister may too often be impelled to defend official conduct when the real need is for a remedy.
To my Conservative friends I would like to point out the bad situation that was gotten into a few years ago by the then hon. member for Peel in connection with some property at Malton, vis-a-vis George Hees, who was then minister of transport, and the fact that you had the minister in essence denying one of his supporters. There was complete confusion. I believe we had a vote of confidence in this house. We certainly had an issue that was sparked by and interravelled with partisanship on the very kind of issue that would never have been raised if the people with the grievance, the citizens with the grievance, had had a grievance commissioner instead of depending upon their member of parliament. I continue reading this report:
On questions of policy, public and parliamentary recourse to ministers is appropriate and necessary. But when what is at issue is a complaint relating to administration in the public service, more effective channels for public and parliamentary challenge may be devised.
To weigh the urgency of these problems, and, if need be, to devise solutions are the tasks of others. Your commissioners wish only to suggest that, should new safeguards be judged necessary, they may be sought in all three of the historic branches of government. First, the role of the courts in checking the excess of official powers and in providing redress of official wrongs against the subject, may repay examination. Second, in the executive branch itself, there may be greater opportunity for the use of formal processes of inquiry, in which the principles of natural justice are observed, either in reaching or in reviewing administrative decisions that affect the rights and obligations of the citizen.
The third course lies in parliament itself. Procedures might be developed for the closer scrutiny of statutory instruments-the orders in council and regulations by which statutory powers are elaborated and applied. Your commissioners have also noted the growing interest throughout other parliamentary countries in the office of parliamentary commissioner, modelled, with variations, on the long established Swedish ombudsman. The notable success with which this office has been adapted to the needs of the parliament of Denmark, the recent report by a group of eminent jurists in the United Kingdom, the enactment of legislation to establish a parliamentary commissioner in New Zealand, and the creation of machinery for a similar purpose in the United States, all suggest that the parliament of Canada may find here a means of bettering its defence against administrative defects in the public service.
I would like to point out that the Gazette reported, on May 23, 1963, this dispatch from Ottawa:
The government suggested Wednesday that parliament itself make the decision on whether to establish special machinery to protect the little man from bureaucrats.
Justice Minister Chevrier said in the Commons its rules committee might study suggestions of

creating a parliamentary commissioner or ombudsman, such as they had in some Scandinavian and other countries. The ombudsman is an official appointed by a legislature to investigate complaints from the public of cases of alleged highhandedness by government officials. Sweden has two of them, one dealing in civil and the other in military law.
I would like to point out that we have had in Canada, and are still having, as the result of the actions we take here, a proliferation of agencies and boards which operate in areas that affect citizens, particularly with regard to licenses and applications, and which are at arm's length from ministerial control; that is, from political control. It seems to me this is particularly the kind of agency in regard to which grievances develop. I always remember one man down in Kingston who has a bit of inventive genius. He developed a particular kind of helicopter. He was satisfied that it was an excellent helicopter, that it would fly, that it had a number of radical provisions in it that might be of much greater use. But he could not get any certificate of airworthiness, or even freedom to test the craft in the proper kind of circumstances, from the inspectors of the Department of Transport; and he was not able to get any satisfaction at all from any of the normal licensing agencies. He took the matter up with the department, through the minister, and could not get any kind of consideration. Finally he took it up with a whole host of members of parliament through some kind of circulating letter. When enough of us had raised Cain about it, finally something was done.
I have another example with regard to what has happened in my own constituency. There was a lady acting as a matchmaker for her brother, and a friend was brought out from Italy. The arrangement was that her brother and this girl would be married when she got here. The girl arrived here, and for various reasons decided not to go through with the wedding. The prospective sister-inlaw was outraged at this and demanded that the government carry through the normal immigration procedure and return the bride, who did not want to be a bride, to Italy. Various pressures were applied. There were very large families involved on each side in this matter, families that spread their networks out to Winnipeg and down to Toronto, and you had a situation wherein the minister and his officials were being bombarded and pressured by M.P.s from those areas, and with private representations; we even had mayors getting involved in the deal. Finally the minister, with all this pressure-and I do not blame the minister of the time-postponed any decision on it and just let the situation ride. This particular lady felt, and still feels, that she
Proposed Office of Parliamentary Counsel has a considerable grievance in that the law and the regulations of Canada did not apply in this case. This is the kind of case, I suggest, where this lady will never get it out of her head that she had been cheated, and cheated by her government, and her family has been held up to ridicule of a permanent kind that can only be settled by some kind of grievance procedure and some kind of person who is completely detached from both the ministerial framework and the influence of those of us who are politicians.
I do not feel there would be any tremendous number of cases right off the bat. I think every hon. member knows that each one of us will get letters from cranks in our constituencies and also from across the country. We know the kind of person who is always feuding and spatting with government agencies, particularly with the unemployment insurance commission or the workmen's compensation board in the province. It is all very easy to put a lot of these people down as cranks and write them off. But so often this tendency should be slowed up by a realization that you only need one case where there is real merit to make you see that these kind of people should at least have their opportunity.
I think the ombudsman would certainly apply. It is apparent that the British, in considering this matter, have felt that the whole question of ministerial responsibility and the joint responsibility of the cabinet has been a factor in their particular parliamentary set-up which would stand in the way of giving a parliamentary commissioner, a grievance commissioner, in Britain the kind of powers he has been given in the Scandinavian countries. This may very well be so; but we need to define the problem much more clearly. This is really what the motion suggests. We need to pinpoint the kind of things that a grievance commissioner could do. Professor Rowat points out, in effect, that the grievance commissioner could be the Auditor General for, you might say, civil and administrative matters as distinct from bookkeeping, cost and expenditure matters. I think that is a good comparison in that I do believe this person should have the freedom that the Auditor General has, to report to this house, rather than to any special minister. If we had such a parliamentary commissioner reporting to parliament and his report being dove-tailed in with a permanent house committee which met regularly every year, I believe you would really give many people in Canada the feeling that there was, in grievance matters concerning the administration, a court of last resort which would be extremely fair.

Proposed Office of Parliamentary Counsel
Beyond that, Mr. Speaker, there is not much more I want to say in case other hon. members would like to express opinions. I have a great deal of material on the matter. It is my impression that both editorial comment and the general feeling among people in politics are relatively favourable to this idea. It seems to me that what we need to know definitely, and I think it is up to both parliament and the government to find it out, are the limitations we should look for in this kind of office in Canada, so as to produce some concrete proposals as to the kind of legislation which would be required. I hope this study can be undertaken fairly soon, certainly within this parliament. It seems to me that one of the real things which will complement the bill of rights, and in a sense give the bill or rights a great deal of significance which it does not have at the present time where the private citizen is involved, in his relationship with the federal government, is this kind of office of a parliamentary grievance commissioner.

subtopic: SUGGESTED OFFICER TO EXAMINE PUBLIC COMPLAINTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed that the motion the hon. member has had on the order paper for a very long time, and which I gather from his remarks today he has brought forward for several sessions now, has come up for debate today, even though I will not have very much time to discuss it. I am afraid other hon. members will be in no better position since it has come on, so to speak, only at the last minute.
The main credit for popularizing the idea of an ombudsman in this country should go, as the hon. member suggested, to Professor Rowat of Carleton University, who did a very extensive study, during the course of a tour of Europe on a Canada council fellowship, of the practice in the European countries which have an ombudsman, and who has published a good many of his findings. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) did not mention-so I thought I would, in case other hon. members are interested-the most comprehensive of Professor Rowat's articles, which is the one to be found in the November 1962 issue of the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science. There has also been some writing on the subject by other academics. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) has just told me that the former member for Rosedale of some years ago, Charles Henry, Q.C., has been taking the initiative on behalf of the Ontario section of the Canadian Bar Association in studying the possibility of introducing the ombudsman scheme to Canada. It is of course, appropriate both at the federal and at the provincial level.


I have not time to go into the history of why such a parliamentary commissioner is necessary. Suffice to say that, with the great growth in discretionary powers at the administrative level of government, there has been a lot of feeling for some time that there should be some way by which the citizen could question by way of appeal the fairness, possibly even the reasonableness, of decisions which are taken in relation to him. We do not have a system of administrative courts in this country. We have the income tax appeal board, which is a type of court, but we do not have too many bodies like this. Even in those cases where we do, there are lots of grievances and problems which citizens have, which for one reason or another can never be brought before these tribunals.
Some European countries which already have a system of administrative courts have also felt the need for a parliamentary commissioner or ombudsman who would be the spokesman or the grievance commissioner for the average citizen. It is not, of course, the complete answer to the problem of the control of discretionary powers. As the royal commission on government organization pointed out, much more needs to be done both within parliament and within the administrative process itself, to try to bring us up to date and to ensure democratic control over administrative discretion. But I do agree with the hon. member that an ombudsman or a parliamentary commissioner or commissioners-I think Professor Rowat suggested that a commission of three would be appropriate in this parliament-should be set up.
The committee on procedure, which has already been established and which, I would hope, will be re-established in another session, will be taking under consideration- again I hope-the possibility of establishing an ombudsman or a comparable officer in this parliament. Indeed, if this is done, the committee should hold public hearings for those of us in parliament who would like to speak much more fully on this matter than we have time for today, and for those academics, lawyers and interested groups in society generally to present their views on the matter. I should think that a thorough series of public hearings would prove extremely useful before initiating a scheme like this; and as I say, I hope that if we go into a new session the committee on procedure will be set up again and will carry out this investigation.
In the meantime, may I make one suggestion to hon. members, and that is that they collect the major types of grievances they have received from their constituents

and build up a file of them. Because in the United Kingdom one of the reasons the ombudsman scheme has tended to be shot down is that they have said there: You have not given enough specific examples of what an ombudsman would do; there have not been detailed grievances specified where citizens have suffered at the hands of the administrative process. I suggest it would be unfortunate if that were to happen here, because I am sure that I, as well as the rest of us here, have many illustrations of cases where individuals have a genuine grievance vis-avis the administration, and we will undoubtedly find more during the recess. I hope it will be possible for this matter to be discussed formally at hearings before the committee on procedure, and that all members of parliament will take an interest in this new parliamentary institution. I suggest that we leave it there, for the moment at any rate, and if all is well the decision to do something about it may well be made, and should be made, in the fairly near future.

Many of these amendments concern matters to which we have given consideration in the past and I think that on the whole they commend themselves to the favourable consideration of the house.
One could make long and prolix speeches, if he wished, about the services rendered by these various organizations. I am thinking particularly of the tax appeal board. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) might give some consideration to the reorganization of that board so as to place it more or less on a permanent basis, similar to that of the courts. After all, when this board was first established it was set up to deal with petty and minor income tax cases. Now it is dealing with cases involving very large sums. I have been conscious, ever since the days when I was connected with the Department of National Revenue, that careful consideration should be given to this particular board. I am sure the same applies to many of the other boards we are considering tonight, and without taking the time of the house further I wish to express support for the principle involved, as far as we are concerned.
It is, of course, for the government to take responsibility for the amounts of the increases recommended. We are prepared to accept the principle that there should be increases in the salaries paid to the members of these various boards and corporate structures. I deplore the fact that in doing so it should be necessary to amend five, ten or 15 statutes at a time, on the basis of one bill. When I was practising law-and perhaps, one day, the Secretary of State will himself be practising law in Bonavista-Twillingate- I was conscious that when considering a bill which set out to amend some 15 statutes, an advocate did not know where to turn or what to do. However, I realize that where the primary and, it seems, the only concern is with the salaries paid, there is scarcely any alternative open and we are prepared to accept it. It is a practice which all governments have followed; we followed it, too, though some of us regretted the practice. I think the principle involved here is sound and to be commended to the house.
