speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we notice that this bill requests a salary increase for a number of people employed in the civil service of Canada. When the persons concerned are competent, we do not object to their obtaining a salary increase, but in the present case, an increase is requested for many classes of employees and I
5958	HOUSE OF
Salaries of Certain Public Officials must say that we, in this corner of the house, object to clause 3 of Bill C-128.
We would rather have a distinct bill; we would have liked that clause 3 be taken out of this bill, that is as far as the salary increase for the chairman of the income tax division is concerned.
Among all the civil servants, he surely is the last one to deserve an increase; he would rather deserve a kick in the pants, as also those responsible for income tax in the province of Quebec, especially.
It was established last year that it was the least well administered of all the federal departments' divisions.
Tax inspectors go around in rural areas, conduct so-called inquiries into charity receipts and declare their inquiries over without having even consulted with the persons concerned. They reduce the amount of charity receipts, especially in the province of Quebec, and then they write the taxpayer: "Dear sir, you have produced charity receipts to the amount of $500 but, on inquiry, we can allow $250 only." What an inquiry. They have not even seen the person concerned. That is the way things are done by those income tax officers.
It is proposed to increase the salary of the chairman, the assistant chairman and the other members of the income tax division. This means that, afterwards, the salary of the other employees of that division will be also increased. We cannot agree to those increases in salaries; as to the other cases, it is all right, but not these, we cannot agree.
Those persons whose salary we are now asked to increase show an unwarranted zeal in the province of Quebec, and everywhere else in Canada, so as to make themselves noticed. Inquiries are made on small merchants and small businessmen, every record is investigated, every small detail is looked into in the hope of finding something wrong. And often, after a two or three week check, an error of $10 or $15 is found.
It is the small businessman who will then have to foot the bill.
That is what we cannot accept, Mr. Speaker. In the long run, it is always the small businessman who is hounded by those officials of the income tax divisions whose salaries it is now proposed to increase. Members of the income tax board prepare a case against Canadian citizens and hand down a sort of judgment without too much investigation. If the citizen is not satisfied, he is the one who has to appeal the judgment. However, since he is not familiar with the law, he does not want to get involved in a costly appeal of the decision of those officials whose salary is to be increased. He merely grumbles against the


Income Tax Act and the people who enforce it, namely those for whom we are considering a pay boost.
It is for that reason and many others, because the members of the income tax division are far from giving satisfaction to the Canadian taxpayers that we are against any pay increase in their case.
We would even say that their salaries should be reduced. That is why, when we come to section 3 of the Bill No. C-128, we intend to move an amendment to reduce the salary of the chairman, the assistant chairman and the members of the income tax division.
It is my feeling that they have shown themselves unable to put themselves at the same level as the general public.
As the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) stated, they behave like extortioners of taxes. That is why, especially those who head that division, who give orders such as those received these days by inspectors with regard to receipts for charitable donations, do not deserve any salary increase, but rather a decrease.
The parliamentary secretary who is the sponsor of Bill No. C-128 should withdraw clause 3 from it so as to make a different bill. If he were to do so, I am convinced that all members of the house would be glad to consign it to oblivion.
If we compare the salary of those gentlemen which is to be increased, and those paid to persons who perform their duties much better, like interpreters, translators and house reporters, it is readily realized that they are out of all proportion.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make at this time. I reserve the right to move an amendment in that connection when we come to section 3.

Mr. Speaker, for a minute or two I should like to direct the attention of the house to one aspect of the bill. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), with his usual lucidity, has spoken for the party and I agree with what he has said. I am concerned about the continuing disparity in the salary paid to

the lieutenant governor of Prince Edward Island. Of all the provinces, I see that the lieutenant governor of that province is in a separate category. If I may make a confession, over the last six years I pleaded and endeavoured to cajole and argue with the former minister of finance, not the member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings but his predecessor, to no avail, and now it would seem that this legislation will not only continue the disparity but will enlarge it.
I do not see that there is any principle proclaiming why one province should be singled out. I will not argue the merits of the case at this stage. I could point out that Prince Edward Island is heading for one of the greatest celebration years in its history. I could point out too that there is probably no province in the country in which the citizenry are in closer contact with government house than in Prince Edward Island. I am sure the Solicitor General, my colleague from Prince, would agree with that.
It is the matter of principle I am concerned about. The salaries obviously are not on a per capita basis because you would not find British Columbia and Newfoundland in the same category. I as a private member cannot initiate steps to remedy this, but I appeal to the sponsor of the bill and the government. I am not saying whether they should bring the others down or put the province of Prince Edward Island up, but I do not see any justification for this discrimination. I never did get a satisfactory answer from the former minister of finance, and I am still alarmed and disturbed at this continuing discrimination.
I will not argue about the relationship of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to the others. If it were not the yuletide season I would even argue about that; but with regard to the other eight it is most disconcerting to me to find the province of Prince Edward Island placed in a separate and lower category than the others. This is improper, and I would appeal to the government to rectify the error. I do not know how it came about. Perhaps the Secretary of State or the parliamentary secretary can give us the historic background on this seeming discrimination. I am very proud of the fact that in the face of many provinces having surrendered the official residences of their lieutenant governors Prince Edward Island, a small province, has through the years maintained its beautiful government house. It was not easy for a small province to do that. So I would hope that in a gesture of appreciation therefor, and of justice long delayed, my suggestion will commend itself to the

First of all, while I am answering the question off the top of my head, I am pretty sure that the salaries of the chairman and officers of the wheat board are settled by the wheat board itself and are not fixed by statute. 1 notice that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who knows more about this than I do, is nodding his head in approval.

speechtext:
-and I have refreshed my memory with regard to the history of our country. I find it rather odd that two years ago, in 1961, the house accepted very favourably the proposition then before it, namely, the setting up of the National Centennial Council. The people who were then in opposition and who are now on the treasury benches spoke very favourably of the suggestion that was advanced by the prime minister of that day. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) all participated in that debate two years ago and found nothing at all wrong with the bill.
At that time the present Prime Minister said:
A centenary is a.. .momentous occasion in the history of a state.
He went on to say:
Our nation will soon be celebrating its one hundredth birthday anniversary.
5962	HOUSE OF
National Centennial Act
The Minister of Transport used the phrase, "at this point in our national progress," and the Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke about, "the beginnings of our nation when we celebrate its one hundredth birthday." The hon. member for Hull used these words:
All the politicians put aside party feeling to bring forth the fullest national unity possible.
That was the spirit two years ago with regard to the celebrations we hope to hold in Canada in 1967. There was no dissenting voice. There was no niggling objection to the use of any word. It was only this year, in 1963, that we discovered there were some objections, and so the government introduced a resolution followed by this bill, to make certain changes.
Strangely enough the people who have spoken on behalf of the government in the debate up to the present have been the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamon-tagne) the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). The resolution stood in the name of the Prime Minister. In view of what he said in 1961 I would have thought he would have taken the resolution and the bill through the house on this occasion, lifted the debate to the high level that pertained two years ago, and drawn the attention of the Canadian people to our great history and the celebrations we hope to hold in 1967, with a look to the future. There was a chance for great leadership, such as was shown in 1961; but this year, 1963, the Prime Minister did not participate, has not participated up to this point; and I wish he would.
He left the job to the President of the Privy Council who introduced the resolution and the bill without any lift to the spirit at all. He pretended that only minor amendments were being made, which led the Secretary of State on to say that it was just an exercise in semantics. Consider the irresponsibility of a government bringing an exercise in semantics before the House of Commons.
I thought the President of the Privy Council was rather careless in his handling of this whole problem. He drew our attention to the fact that certain changes were desirable in the translation into French, and he said that those changes could have been made by the former administration. I ask him, why could those changes, to which we raise no objection, not have been made in the French version, if it was inaccurately translated originally, as he stated, instead of making a major change in the bill and, through his casual introduction, stirring up discord on a matter which should have no element of discord in it? Why could he not have done that, when what we are talking about is our country, our native 

land, the birth of our nation; and I am using the word "nation" in the sense in which people of English speech use it? We got the word from the French and it came originally from the Latin. There may be other meanings to the word nation but with us we consider it, and have done so for a long time, as the designation of a political entity covering an area, and all the divers peoples who are united together in that political entity.
Why could not the president of the council, when pointing out to us that there were some feelings among our French speaking brethren about the translation, have made that correction, instead of making a much more substantial change by way of the one which was introduced into the house? He has, by his actions-and he is acting, of course, as spokesman for the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)- raised a certain discord which is incompatible with the nature of the future celebrations that we hope to hold in this country. What purpose is served by this type of activity? I think that upon reflection the Prime Minister and the president of the council would be ready to express regret that they did not follow the course that was so carefully plotted in 1961, and keep the whole discussion of this interesting subject on a very, very high level. Not content with doing that, the President of the Privy Council distorted history on November 20. He used these words, as is reported on page 4979 of Hansard:
It is quite clear to me, as it should be to the right hon. gentleman, that our nation and Canada existed before 1867. What did happen in 18877 United Canada and two other separate British colonies joined together in a confederation to form a single British colony, which became sovereign in fact much later in the present century.
I suggest that is a distortion of history.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No one is prepared to say there was not a Canadian nation before 1867. Also, if you like, there was an English nation in this country before 1867; but we do not use that term at all. At the time of confederation one of the great leaders of that era, who was quoted by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was speaking on this subject, used these words:
The time has arrived to form a great nation. If we unite, we will form a political nationality independent of the national origin and religion of individuals.
We have always accepted that as the historical fact with regard to what happened in 1867. And the other fathers of confederation were not talking about forming a larger British colony; they were talking about forming a new state comprised of the former British colonies that were on the North American continent. They were thinking in terms of a new state. Their opposite numbers in the British Isles were thinking along the same lines. When the secretary of the colonies, Lord Carnarvon, was discussing the British North America Act on February 19, 1867, he used these words:
We are laying the foundation of a great state- perhaps one which at a future day may even overshadow this country.
Mr. Adderley, who was a distinguished member of the British House of Commons, said this:
The rest of this large continent, still British, is now asking us to assist them to develop their own strength and resources in retained connection and in partnership of allegiance to one common sovereign.
Mr. Cardwell, who had been in the former administration secretary of the colonies and was subsequently minister of defence, used these words:
Time was when it was the policy of this country to exercise a strong imperial control over her colonies. If that policy continued it would be unwise to pass this bill...but that policy has now passed away and the sole object of our government now is to have the satisfaction, pride and pleasure of witnessing the growth under the crown of England of great and powerful communities attached to the mother country by no other ties than those of love and affection and a reciprocal regard, which will prove a source of strength in the hour of danger.
Mr. Gladstone, on March 28, 1867, said:
It is impossible to conceive anything more complete than our acknowledgment of those rights of self-government.
He was referring to the changed conditions that were being brought about in Canada. Then he said:
We have carried it to this point, that as far as regards the administration, I believe it may be said that the only officer appointed by the colonial secretary is the governor; and I believe there
National Centennial Act cannot be a doubt that if it were the well ascertained desire of the colonies to have the appointment of their own governor, the imperial parliament would at once make over to them that power.
There is nothing, sir, in the evidence of the debates in Canada at the time of confederation, or in the debates in the British house of commons, to indicate that just a larger British colony was being formed. It was the creation of a new state, with complete independence; and any vestiges of colonialism that were left in Canada were due to Canadians themselves. The chief vestige that was left from 1867 to 1871 was the presence in Canada of a considerable force of British soldiers who were kept here at the request of the Canadian government because of the threat of the Fenian raids from across the border. I hope that the national centennial council, when it makes its plans for 1967, will commemorate in some form or other the assistance and sacrifice of the long suffering British taxpayer who supported numerous British troops in Canada from 1867 to 1871 before the four million people who then comprised Canada were ready to undertake the responsibilities which certainly rested upon them.
I suggest it is wrong to distort history by pretending, as has been pretended now for so many years, that Canada was just a colony of Great Britain after 1867. For 25 years before that time self-government had been accorded the British colonies on the North American continent. We became a nation state in 1867, and that is the point in time to which we are looking back, to celebrate in 1967. The people of 100 years ago in Canada and in Great Britain looked forward with vision to the future and saw the development of a great self-governing dominion, which was almost called kingdom, on the British North American continent. Everything that Canada wanted by way of independence the people in Great Britain were prepared to give. So I suggest that the President of the Privy Council is distorting history in making the suggestion that he does.
Now I have a much more serious point to bring to the attention of the house. I have already indicated that in the debate so far, in marked contrast with the debate in 1961, the only people who have spoken on the government side are the president of the council, the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Lotbiniere. I take it that, this being a government measure, these people were speaking on behalf of the government, and were setting out the policy of the government and of the Liberal party. At the time I adjourned the debate on November 21 I did so because, having listened

National Centennial Act very carefully to the speech of the hon. member for Lotbiniere, I thought that the right of reply should be accorded to people on this side of the house.
Let us consider, Mr. Speaker, some of the things said by the hon. member during the course of that debate. I heard him speak, but Hansard does not record the eloquence of his remarks, the fervour with which they were presented to the house and the emphasis that he placed upon them. Let us consider very carefully what he said. He picked upon the most important change in the bill, and as reported at page 5006 said this:
But the most Important change, in my opinion, is the new name that is proposed. Instead of celebrating the centennial of the nation, we are going to celebrate the centennial of confederation. Of course that implies rather different circumstances, because we are ready to celebrate the Canadian nation at any time, but to celebrate the centennial of confederation, that is not exactly the same thing.
So he based his remarks on this main portion of the act. Then in his peroration, which was very well delivered, he speaks with feeling and with fire. He went on in these words:
Canada is an economic power; it has the right to transact business freely with other countries. It declared war in 1939-which is a sign of total Independence-and since 1945, it has its own representative at the United Nations. Why should it still be subject to bonds of colonialism?
Thus he harped on the theme set out earlier by the President of the Privy Council, on the theme of colonialism, which is a misreading of history and is false to the history of our country. Then, Mr. Speaker, here is his final paragraph:
Here is the nonsensical situation in which Canada finds herself in 1963: without a flag, without a national anthem, unable to amend its own constitution in some cases and a foreign sovereign is the symbol of its supreme authority.
Those were the words of the hon. member for Lotbiniere speaking, I took it, on behalf of the government, setting out the policy of the Liberal government. I call upon the Prime Minister of this country to come into this house and to make a statement. Does he agree with these words of the hon. member for Lotbiniere? Is that the stand that he takes with regard to this country? Or has he some different idea which he would like to put before the Canadian people? Will he speak in the terms in which he spoke in 1961?
Mr. Speaker, until I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Lotbiniere and the remarks of the President of the Privy Council on second reading, I was constrained to consider that the changes proposed, much as we regretted them, might be accepted; but I have reached the conclusion that we are

being pushed a bit too far under the circumstances. I suggest to the Prime Minister of this country and to the members of the Liberal party that they reconsider their position. There is no one in Canada who is not proud of his country; and we use the word "country" as synonymous with "state" and "nation". There is no Canadian who is not proud of this country. There is no Canadian who does not like the idea-I hope-of celebrating the one hundredth anniversary of our country. This is something to lift the heart, raise the spirits and enable us to look to the future. At the time we do celebrate our one hundredth birthday, let us review the whole history, the prior history, of this great country of Canada. Why not? It is a fascinating history, and so many races have contributed to the development of Canada. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) pointed out the contributions which had been made by people not belonging to the two original founding races. The whole opening up of western Canada, a vast empire in itself, has been due in very large part to the activity and dedication of people of races neither English nor French.
If we are going to have, or continue to have, as I think we have had in the past, a united Canada, why should we be exposed to the type of activity foisted upon us by the President of the Privy Council, who could have brought in the necessary amendment to the French translation of the act and left us with what we thought was established two years ago? Nobody in Canada two years ago, at the time the act was presented to the House of Commons, raised any objection. These objections came subsequently.

In 1961. This whole idea was grasped with enthusiasm by the people of this country. And now the president of the council, speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, has brought discord into the discussion of something which should have been so much above that. This, I think, is deplorable. National Centennial Act this bill has nothing to do with that matter at all. The purpose of this bill is to make certain corrections in the French text of the act, to make certain other consequential amendments, and quite properly to take advantage of this situation to change certain expressions which have given offence in certain parts of this country, and to substitute other expressions which, it seems to me, can give no reasonable offence to anyone. I would hope we would all try, no matter where objections come from in this country-if people are sensitive about certain things, and if those objections can be overcome without creating irritation in other quarters-I hope we would all try to meet those objections. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre indicated in his opening remarks, I hope we shall not seek to exacerbate any differences there may be in connection with this matter but that, instead, we shall deal with the words and the expressions which are actually in the bill before us, so that any irritation or misunderstanding which may have been caused can be overcome as quickly as possible.
We all know, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre hinted, that the word "nation" in the English language is generally used as a synonym for the word "state". We also know that in the French language it has two senses. Out of this comes, sometimes, misunderstanding. We also know that the word "foreigner" in English is translated in French by the word "dtranger". There was one occasion when Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who had an almost perfect command of the English language-it was not a perfect command; indeed, few of us have a perfect command even of our own mother tongue-used the word "foreigner" when all he meant was the word "stranger", and thereby caused a tremendous commotion, though a person thoroughly familiar with both languages would easily have understood what had happened.
We in this country have a problem because we do have two official languages, but it seems to me that even those of us in this house who are familiar with only one of them should try to understand both the potentialities and the limitations of the other language, and try to make as much accommodation for them as possible. It seems to me that only in that way can we have the united country that we want to see; only in that way can we celebrate, in 1967 what I like to call, in the words of the British North America Act, the union which took place in that year.

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to hear the

If I may make a suggestion to the government which wants to appoint a new Canadian ambassador to London, it should appoint to that post the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on account of the assertions he has just made, in order to rid Canada of him.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot with a mere stroke of the pen, cross out 200 years of history, that is the two centuries which elapsed before confederation took place in 1867. We may have been able to create a confederation of two nations in 1867, but it takes more than a day to build a nation.
The founding of a country comes gradually as events go on and is the result of a succession of events which preceded it. It develops through all sorts of legislation which precede it. There were final statutes before the 1867 act, namely the act of Quebec in 1774, another legislation in 1791, one in 1842 and finally confederation in 1867.
A country is not founded overnight. Before confederation, we had a whole series of outstanding facts, of leaders in the political and cultural fields, etc. Natural resources were developed which enabled the country to develop by itself.
It is the blending of all those facts which made it possible to designate at one particular time the 1867 act by the name of confederation. But that was not the foundation of a new state nor the creation of a new nation. It was a progression through circumstances, facts and developments which made it possible for Upper and Lower Canada, having come to maturity, to form what we call today the Canadian confederation.
We can take as an example Algeria, which has just reached independence. Would it be right to say that Algeria has become a nation over night merely on account of the fact that France has given it its independence? Obviously not, for previous to that, there had been historic events, personalities and cultural developments. That is what made possible the formation of a new country and a new nation.
The same thing could be said of the Congo and of those Latin American countries which, for years, have evolved by themselves through their own culture and with the support of other colonial countries which succeeded in opening up new cultural vistas for them. After a series of events, the adoption of various pieces of legislation and the appearance


of men who succeeded in imposing their personality, a new way of life was born in those countries. New legislation was the concrete evidence of all past efforts.
Confederation, Mr. Speaker, did not come into being spontaneously. It was not spontaneous generation nor a new state. It was the result of centuries of efforts, work and development. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, a former minister, must not find in the fact that a piece of legislation is being changed an excuse for a political debate.
We speak of confederation. A confederation is not born out of nothing, it comes out of something that existed beforehand. That is what gave birth to confederation. It is because some things existed before that those things could be united to form confederation. It is not a union of nothing, a union in a vacuum, but a union of principles, factors, human resources and natural resources, which at a given moment formed confederation.
Since it is a confederation built on principles, cultures, personalities and legislation that already existed, it was possible to make a concrete whole out of those things and to form confederation. There, Mr. Speaker, you have a confederation born out of something which exists.
Reference is made to the confederation centennial, to a nation. A while ago, I wanted to challenge the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who, in doing so, was actually taking to task the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) also deemed it advisable, after the Prime Minister, to repudiate the statement made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. I do not mean to say that I approve 100 per cent the idea as expressed by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. But there is perhaps one thing that should be borne in mind. If a nation, in the sense the word is used by English speaking Canadians, a political nation, is to be built, we French Canadians believe it must be given an image in keeping with a real nation. How is that image of a nation which exists by itself to be achieved? At the present time, we have a geographical image of our country, with boundaries to the east, west, north and south. But, in the interior, what is the image of this country? Let us look at our public buildings. Were we able to give them names representing symbols for Canadians as Canadians? As a matter of fact, when the question of choosing a name for an hotel in Montreal came up, it was called Queen Elizabeth.
I agree, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) stated the other day, that the Queen of England is also the Queen of Canada, that she is bilingual and nice, but if

we want to create the image of a Canadian country, why not give our public buildings names which represent something for Canadians, as Canadians and for Canada, as a country?
Let us look, for instance, at the name given to the street right in front of the parliament buildings in Ottawa: Wellington street, a name which recalls a great English general.
Put your hand in your pocket and take out your paper money. What are you going to find on it? Again the picture of the Queen.
Put a stamp on an envelope. The same picture again.
Streets, parks, public buildings are our symbols. Do we manage really to create a Canadian image favourable to each and everyone of the Canadian citizens? Are we trying to unite the Canadian people?
Here is another example, Mr. Speaker. About a fortnight ago, I had the opportunity to watch the Grey cup game on television. An interesting game, I agree, but it started with a regiment parading with the union jack while "God Save the Queen" was being played. Should anyone doubt the truth of what I am saying, let him get the tape recordings of that T.V. program and he will see that I am right. It was beautiful since it happened in Vancouver, but I, watching that television program in Jonquiere, that is, at the other end of the country, I heard the national anthem of another country whereas they displayed the flag of another country. What does it do for Canada?
Mr. Speaker, all that gives food for thought when we speak about celebrating the centennial of confederation, which others call the nation. Have we really created an image of the Canadian nation which displays the feeling of each and every Canadian? Or have we not, for too long and too often, drawn from foreign symbols?
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the points I wanted to make. I made these remarks as they came to my mind, particularly following the speech just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). I would have liked to answer some of the other remarks he made tonight, for I must admit I was somewhat surprised to hear them, particularly at a time when Canadians make a real effort towards understanding between the two great nations.
Recently, we saw-and I believe this is really relevant to the centennial of confederation, soon to be celebrated-the president of the Canadian National Railways suggest a program to promote bilingualism and bicul-turalism in our country, a program which was unanimously adopted. In fact, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and the hon.
National Centennial Act member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) seconded a motion I put forward to support that policy, which may be was only a project, but the results of which will be evaluated later on.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, steps towards understanding. But if speeches like that made tonight by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre were heard too often, then we would go backwards, retracing our steps continually.
The other day, the hon. member for Three Rivers deemed it advisable to make a speech on the state of Quebec during the debate on a motion I had presented. I am wondering if he will have the nerve to rise tonight and protest against the arguments raised a while ago by one of his former cabinet colleagues, namely the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.
I am wondering also if the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) will raise his arms as high today as he usually does when he is putting questions to the Prime Minister or the President of the Privy Council, and if he will protest with all the vigour called for against the speech we heard a short while ago?
You will read the speech I made some time ago.

Mr. Speaker, it is very well to make nice speeches but you must also practice what you preach. If you let the arguments heard tonight go unchallenged, you can say that these are high-sounding speeches, principles being formulated, and that you do not want things to go any farther. In fact, you must not be afraid to protest if need be, even if members of your own party are involved.
Mr. Speaker, these things must be said to put the cards on the table and stop allowing those who do not want understanding or who want to break open doors to come here and make speeches like the one we heard tonight.
If it is the wish to appoint the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre as Canadian ambassador to England, I would be the first to second the motion. This would be an opportunity to send him for some time in another country.
Mr. Speaker, one of the best ways to celebrate properly the centennial of confederation would be to set about preparing it seriously. Recently, efforts were made to promote bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada. There is an exchange of ideas and I conclude my remarks by emphasizing this point. Let us not forget that the most important problem at the present time-

Hear, hear.

National Centennial Act

Mr. Speaker, I notice that there are still a few backbenchers who did not understand; in short, they are ignorant. But when time comes for these hon. members to speak about wheat, then they can talk for 24 hours. And since we let them outline their problems, they should be as broadminded as we are and let us enjoy the same privilege.
Mr. Speaker, the last problem I want to raise is the most important, I think, since confederation. I mean the taxation problem which brushes aside all the others and about which our English speaking colleagues seem to have fallen into step. In my opinion, this problem must be settled if we do not want to witness the breaking off of confederation, even before the centennial celebration. The parties concerned must get together and settle the problem, so as to enable us to save confederation whose centennial we want to celebrate in four years from now.

Mr. Speaker, just a few remarks.
We have been listening tonight to two speeches which, instead of being sources of agreement, are precisely sources of dissension.
As one complains on the one hand that some people lack breadth of outlook, on the other hand, one can complain about the same things even though one must keep those complaints for oneself.
I suggest that truths have been told tonight but that they could or should have been told in other circumstances. I believe that what we need is action rather than claims made at the top of one's voice, inconsiderately, without taking into account circumstances or varied factors that should be of interest to everybody.
Some say we should be acting instead of making speeches. I think that could be applied to those who talk that way and never do anything.
In a country such as ours, made up of various ethnic groups, of two official groups whose official languages are recognized, I think it is enough to know each other better, to better appreciate each other and to be able to recognize our characteristics in order to get along instead of always blaming each other and saying: if we cannot get along, there will be separation, or you are lacking co-operation.
There is exaggeration on both sides, but without going into more details, I should like to say that there still are probably in this house some people who have sound middle course principles, who know there are problems on both sides and who think it should be possible to find grounds for agreement instead of living in discord.


I think that the changing of this National Centennial Act into the Centennial of Canadian Confederation Act is a step forward towards the settlement of that problem. I think it is not by adopting rigid, unchangeable and die-hard attitudes that we can succeed in solving that problem. It is rather by admitting calmly the things that are done, like the project before us tonight, that we can finally arrive, not at a Canadian unity-it is quite hard to have real unity with so much diversity-but at co-operation and good understanding between the two majority groups which make up our country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am impelled to say a word or two in view of the contribution made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). He, in turn, found it necessary to speak because of earlier speeches that had been made. I was particularly interested in the expression of his views, to which I shall make allusion in a moment, that only those who are members of the cabinet can speak for the Liberal party and the government of the day.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure the right hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. I said that only the members of the cabinet could speak for the government.

Well, I intend to refer to the fact that this cabinet certainly does not live up to the high aspirations that were designated by the minister during the course of his remarks. I think we have had a series of examples recently in this connection which would indicate that the cabinet of today has as many voices as the representations that are made to its membership require it to have. I am going to give some examples of that because I think it would be intensely interesting to understand how a government can express itself in unity, when amongst its members their voices are generally raised in disunity.
However, I am going back to the initial stages of this particular legislation. I introduced this legislation in this house, and it received general support. The then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), gave his views at the time, as did the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith). I am going to read a few of the remarks made by the Prime Minister, and when I read them it will be understood why it is that these amendments are brought in by someone other than the Prime Minister. I do not want to read at length, but I refer to the remarks made by the then leader of the opposition, because I gather that the word "nation" or

"national"-either of these words-have a connotation that denies their use in the interests of national unity.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister, on a point of order.
I challenge the right hon. gentleman to show me where the word "nation" is in the English version of the present act and also to show me that we are deleting the word "national" from the present act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; perhaps I should mention that, in my opinion, that is not a point of order but rather a point of debate.

As a matter of fact it is a point of disorder. I read what the Prime Minister said:
I think all members of this committee wherever they may sit would wish to give wholehearted support to this resolution.
Then he said:
It is perhaps a happy coincidence that the Prime Minister on his sixty sixth birthday anniversary should be reminding us that our nation will soon be celebrating its one hundredth birthday anniversary. It is appropriate that we should prepare for that celebration.
Then a little later on again he said that Canada as a nation would be 100 years of age; and still later:
The fact that we shall soon be celebrating our hundredth birthday makes us one of the older states in the world.
As the Prime Minister has said, this celebration should encompass the whole range of Canada's history, not merely the achievement of confederation itself.
Then again, as recorded at page 8469 of Hansard for September 18, 1961, he said:
Also, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, it would be appropriate to re-examine the values of our national society.
He spoke. The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) spoke. The Minister of Transport of today spoke; and never was there one word of criticism among any of the members now sitting on the government side when this bill was before the house. They gave it undivided support. There was not one word of criticism in this house, not one word of criticism in the other place. Then, suddenly, ten days or so after the bill became law the first objection was raised by the premier of Quebec, who indicated that he would not permit his province to participate in the celebration of our anniversary unless there were changes made in the legislation.
National Centennial Act
Why was it that those sitting opposite today, when they sat over here, saw nothing wrong then? Why did they support it throughout? Why was there such unanimity, and why the change that took place within a few days after His Excellency had given royal approval? It was only because the premier of Quebec decided that the wording of the legislation did not meet his desires or wishes.
I want to be very clear on this. Over and over again, in an endeavour to bring about national unity within our country, when some of us disagree with other fellow Canadians we are immediately charged with being anti this or that. The suggestion has been made that I am anti-Quebec because I dared to say that I disagreed with Premier Lesage. Is he anti-Canadian because he disagrees with me? Was he anti-Quebec when he disagreed with Premier Duplessis? Surely there must be better arguments advanced than that, that every time you disagree with the premier of one province in Canada you thereby become anti-Quebec?
I was never anti-Quebec at any time.
Hear, hear.

I point this fact out to the President of the Privy Council, that almost 40 years ago I argued a case in the province of Saskatchewan on appeal, whereby school trustees who were prosecuted for the use of the French language had been convicted. It was not a popular stand to take, but my belief was that the French had the right to their language in the schools of Saskatchewan. I took that case and at that time, 40 years ago, there was little thought of my being in politics. Those views represented my views, when it was unpopular to hold those views, and I emphasize that fact; but throughout the years it has been the prerogative of the Liberal party to charge those who may not agree with their viewpoints at any one time as being anti-somebody, anti-something. It is simply a continuation of divide and rule, which for so many years represented the reason for success of the Liberal party.
I was referring to the debate that took place on September 18, 1961. I think that above all in this nation we believe in freedom. We believe in the necessity of the preservation of those things that had their consummation in confederation.
When the Liberal party, under Mr. St. Laurent, was arguing in this house that the rights of language, religion and education guaranteed under the British North America Act could be amended by a majority of this House of Commons and of the Senate, the Conservative party took the stand that the

National Centennial Act rights of French Canadians, their religious and educational rights, were inviolate, unchallengeable and unchangeable. While we took that view, Mr. St. Laurent said that they could be changed by a simple vote of parliament, a principle that this party has never accepted, and which denies the basic agreements between Macdonald and Cartier and those who made confederation-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask a question?

Please, Mr. Speaker; I will be glad when I conclude to answer any question that the hon. gentleman will ask. At the moment I choose to proceed, but he will get every opportunity.
The words of Sir George Etienne Cartier are pertinent today. This is what he said:
The time has arrived to form a great nation, and I maintain that, as far as we are concerned, confederation has become necessary to our commerce, our prosperity, and our protection...
The government is of the opinion that confederation is necessary, but it is ready to hear the honourable members on the other side who apparently intend to oppose it. I am aware that members of this house and a number of people in Upper Canada and the maritime provinces believe that a legislative union would be far more advantageous than a confederation. As far as I am concerned, I believe that a single government could not deal properly with the private and local interests of the various sections or the various provinces. No other system is practicable but a federal system. It is pretended that it will be impossible to carry out confederation on account of differences of race and of religion. Those who hold that opinion are in error. It is precisely on account of the difference in races and local interests that the federal system should be established and that it will work well.
He went on to say a little later on:
Objection is made to our project, because of the words "a new nationality".
But if we unite, we will form a political nationality independent of the national origin and religion of individuals. Some have regretted that we have a distinction of races, and have expressed the hope that, in time, this diversity will disappear. The idea of a fusion of all races is utopian; it is an impossibility. Distinctions of this character will always exist; diversity is the order of the physical, moral and political world. As to the objection that we cannot form a great nation because Lower Canada is French and Catholic, Upper Canada English and Protestant, and the maritime provinces mixed, it is futile.
Then he goes on to say:
We cannot by law make the differences of race disappear, but I am convinced that the Anglo Canadians and the French Canadians will appreciate the advantages of their position. Set side by side, like a great family, their contact will produce a happy spirit of emulation. The diversity of races will in fact, believe me, contribute to the common prosperity.
Hear, hear.

Those words of 1867 by the great tribune of French Canada in confederation are as true today as they were then. 
Ever since there have been divisions from time to time, but the essence of Canada is tolerance in action and in fact, a recognition that while we will not always agree in all things, over and above the disagreements that sometimes separate us is a common dedication to freedom and a recognition that those of the English and the French race, and the other races that have come to this country, each has a part to play, the basic races with their constitutional rights and the other races having that freedom which gives to those of us who are Canadian a pride in the greatness of our citizenship.
Over and over again it has been the history of our country that too often for political purposes divisions have been created. I would like to say it was because I believed in the possibilities in that connection that I advocated the need of the questions in dispute on national symbols, and the like, being submitted to a dominion-provincial conference; a conference representative of all the political parties of the nation and of all the races of the nation-because no matter what the symbols may be, they cannot be pushed on to the people; they must be accepted nationally, by our people as a whole. In other words, there must be that feeling that each and all are endeavouring to bring about that Canadian citizenship, strong, vital and free. I think of the words of Sir Charles George Douglas Roberts, when considering some of the things that have happened in the last year or so in our country. I think these words are so applicable:
Awake my country, the hour is great with change.
In other words, let us-and I make this Plea-fight our political battles over the things that separate us; but do not let us start fighting political battles in order to get votes over the questions that separate us and are bound to separate us from time to time because of the different racial origins of our country.
Hear, hear.

Again I quote Cartier, who said this:
-there will be Catholics and Protestants, English, French, Irish and Scotch, and each by its efforts and success will add to the prosperity of the dominion and to the glory of the new confederation. We are of different races, not to quarrel but to work together for the common welfare.
That was the spirit of Cartier and of Macdonald and of Laurier; and that is the spirit that we need today. But for some reason the President of the Privy Council has belonged to those that in the past several years have continued to activate division in this country.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not so.

Oh, yes. I cannot understand why it is that what was right on September 18 and later in September of 1961, what was accepted thereafter until changed by the premier of Quebec, suddenly becomes wrong, suddenly becomes discordant, suddenly brings about a division in the nation. I plead with the government that in these things we do not proceed in a way that can only leave wounds. I am not going to say more in that connection, but I point out once more that there was unanimity when the legislation was passed; there was acceptance. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) joined in the band, and, now-
What about consultation with the provinces?

-what was good in 1961 has become an element of disunity in 1963. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) was going to ask me a question a little earlier. I will be glad to answer it, and then I want to say something about the cabinet in a kindly way.

speechtext: My question will, I think, be entirely non-contentious. The right hon. gentleman referred to a statement made by Mr. St. Laurent in 1949 about section 133 of the British North America Act. I am asking the right hon. gentleman whether when he made that statement he had forgotten that this same Mr. St. Laurent, in this house in the autumn of 1949, proposed an amendment to the British North America Act No. 2 of 1949, which safeguarded it for all time and took it beyond the power of a simple majority to do that. And to be fair to Mr. St. Laurent it should be pointed out that the defect he had mentioned in the constitution, he himself took the initiative in removing.

Mr. Speaker, I said that Mr. St. Laurent had stated that by a simple amendment of parliament those rights could be taken away. We said no, and then finally Mr. St. Laurent asked parliament to amend the British North America Act so as to remove the doubt which was in his mind, but never in ours in this party. I mentioned Sir Wilfrid Laurier a moment ago and I want to quote what he said, because I think it might be studied with interest by the President of the Privy Council:
Below the island of Montreal the water that comes from the north, from the Ottawa, unites with the waters that come from the great lakes to the west, but uniting they do not mix. They run parallel, separate, distinguishable, and yet they are one stream, flowing within the same banks of the mighty St. Lawrence, and rolling on toward the sea...
National Centennial Act
There is the perfect image of our nation. We may not assimilate, we may not blend, but for all that we are the component parts of the same country. We may be French in origin, we may be English or Scots or whatever, but we are Canadian-one in aim and one in purpose.
That represents the view that this party has always taken from the days of confederation, to which it contributed so much and has continued to do so throughout the years since.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) gave us a lesson in cabinet solidarity and responsibility, and told us how only the members of the government can speak for the government. I was quite interested in that, because we have had some examples in the last while which indicate that he has not been studying the situation as carefully as he might. In his speech on April 23 the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) used these words, which were to be descriptive of the events which would take place in Canada within the 60 days and thereafter. These are challenging words:
This is a time to excite the daring, test the strong and give new promise to the timid.
They are striking words and they had national appeal. I am going to refer to some of the things which have happened recently in this regard-because the Secretary of State has chosen to bring this question up-and to indicate the unity which prevails over there.
This government, Mr. Speaker, is a collection of ministers who dispense contradictory statements about confusing policies. It is a government of uncertainty wherein each minister voices his private opinions publicly. It is a government in which principles or consistencies are not regarded as important. It is a government wherein the ministers, in a spirit of diplomacy, agree with whatever representations are being made at the moment. I am going to refer to some examples of this. We have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) who, rumour has it, is about to take a diplomatic post. Well, he showed high powers of diplomacy the other day when the labour group met with him. This labour organization group asked for sweepstakes for the-
On a point of order; could we come back to the discussion of the second reading of this bill?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if we had ample time there would be a great deal I would like to say on this item. I know the minister is anxious to get away but I do want to bring to the attention of the house some matters in connection with this item. The minister gave an excellent address to the Saskatchewan river development association on November 1 of this year at Moose Jaw, the title of the address being "Energy From Water". I wish to quote briefly from this address because I think these remarks are well worth putting on the record. The minister said, commencing at page 6:
This makes it imperative that every available drop of water must be used wisely. Waste is inexcusable even in the midst of plenty, but where an increasing demand approaches the limit of the available supply, waste is not inexcusable, it is suicidal.
The warning signals are being given us by many people whose reputations are such as to command our most serious attention. Among them Mr. David Cass-Beggs, general manager of the Saskatchewan Power Corporation, has recently said that it can almost be taken for granted that in the next 30 years or less much of the flow of the Peace and the Athabaska will have been diverted into the North Saskatchewan and in part into the South Saskatchewan. In addition to conserving and redirecting water flows from the eastern side of the continental divide Mr. Cass-Beggs has suggested the most serious study of proposals to use diversion of water from the west side of the Rocky mountains into the southern river systems where they are most needed. It is quite certain that to many Canadians who have always associated water with plenty, such proposals will smack of popular mechanics. They should remember that these forebodings, in time it is to be hoped, overdrawn if some would prefer to call them so, may deliver us from the crises by which water failures have pockmarked the pages of world history and even at this moment are threatening great areas of this continent. The conservation or wise use of our water resources should be the concern of every citizen.
I am sure everybody will agree with the minister's contention in that respect as those remarks were made directly applicable to the water requirements of the prairie provinces. Because of its keen appreciation of these circumstances the government of Saskatchewan had some surveys made under the direction of Mr. Cass-Beggs of the Saskatchewan Power Corporation as to the possibility of diverting some of the waters on the western side of the Rockies and in northern areas of the prairies

into the North Saskatchewan and into the South Saskatchewan. The result of these surveys was published in a paper called "Energy And Water For Western Canada" by Mr. Cass-Beggs. In that connection I want to quote one paragraph and then make a few concluding remarks. On page 5 of this very interesting report there is a paragraph headed "Water Supply and Demand" which reads as follows:
It is well known that the prairie provinces- Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba-are the most arid parts of Canada, particularly in the settled areas. It is not generally realized, however, how serious a problem the future water supply to these areas may be. The original source of water in a drainage basin is of course the total precipitation. But the net water available is the run-off after evaporation and transpiration by vegetable life has returned a proportion to the atmosphere. While the precipitation in the settled part of the prairies is the lowest in Canada, about 17 inches, the run-off remaining as a source of water is a much smaller proportion of the precipitation than in any other region, resulting in only 2.8 inches per annum. This should be compared with 11 inches in Ontario, 15 inches in Quebec and about 25 inches in British Columbia and the maritimes. It might also be noted that the settled areas of the prairies represent some 30 per cent of the settled area of Canada but has only some 6 or 7 per cent of the run-off.
In this study he goes on to indicate how water can be diverted from the Columbia into the South Saskatchewan river system and from the Peace and other rivers into the North Saskatchewan river system. I mention this particularly because the minister has recognized the seriousness of this problem to the prairies, particularly in the future and possibly in the near future, and because Mr. Cass-Beggs and the government of Saskatchewan recognize it. I understand that the governments of Alberta and Manitoba are also concerned. As I mentioned in a question this afternoon, the premier of Saskatchewan has called a conference of ministers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to be held in Regina on December 20, Friday of this week, to give consideration to the water requirements of the prairie provinces. I know that the minister, according to the reply he gave to my question this afternoon, is going to attend this conference. We are very pleased that he is and we hope that when he attends the conference he will give very serious consideration to the views of the representatives of the provinces. We trust that as a result of the conference in Regina the water requirements of the prairie provinces will be assured for all time to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this has been a very involved and, I think for both governments, a somewhat embarrassing question, in that there seemed to be a very honest feeling on the part of the government of Quebec that the demands of industrial developments in what they called "Nouveau Quebec" made it necessary for them to go in and administer the area. Indeed, they have, in respect of the development of lands, control of properties, police and so on. I want to assure the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm that up until very recently the interest of the province of Quebec in that area was practically negligible. Indeed, the federal government had gone in as a result of an award, as I would call it, of the Supreme Court of Canada in 1939 by which they deposed that Eskimos were a tribe of Indians and the federal government had responsibility for looking after them. The federal government has been in there ever since.
I think, in the main, we have done a very good job. We have at present almost $3 million worth of buildings, including schools. The annual cost of education and welfare of the Eskimos of the area amounts to approximately $1,800,000 per year. There was a request by the province of Quebec that we vacate the field to them, including the buildings. I made a trip there to see what the reaction was. I found that the Eskimos made the following demands upon me, that no change from the federal administration to provincial control be made without further consulting them. I found that their opinions were so definite that I told them we would not make a change without discussing the situation further with them. They said that they were eminently pleased with the federal administration; that there had been exceedingly rough times when many people had


starved, and today people were no longer starving. They did not want a change made.
The province of Quebec sent in its officials, and I want to assure my hon. friend we gave instructions immediately to our people on the ground to co-operate with them in every respect. They have done so. I cannot credit that any of our people endeavoured to develop animosity amongst the Eskimos to the people from Quebec, and I do not believe the Hudson's Bay officials have done that. I have no doubt that continuing discussions will take place between us and the province of Quebec. We are quite prepared to go on with those. But I have made this commitment, and I do not want to involve the people who, in the interests of the government here and the government of the province of Quebec, are protecting the Eskimo people in an area where the resources seem very slight indeed. It is an area where a great number of people, I think, would have to be accommodated with houses, because I have seen some there who had no shelter whatever from the weather.
I say the arrangements between the governments, I have found honourable in every respect, and I think they will continue that way in whatever we do.

speechtext: Is it agreed that on Thursday the house will commence its sitting at eleven o'clock in the morning?
Agreed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: This is understood. We agree.
